title: Before
scene: A Chicago morning. Two cups. Fourteen days.

paragraphs: There were two cups on the table and nowhere safe to put either of them.

Aarna had covered the remaining space with exhibition invitations. Outside her Chicago apartment, a delivery truck was reversing into the alley. Its warning sounded three times before someone shouted that there was room.
She moved an invitation from one pile to another. In the morning light the paper looked warmer than it had at the printer's.
Mukund stood in the doorway holding the cups. "Is the paper having both?"
She cleared a rectangle large enough for his cup.
"And yours?"
"I'm holding it."
"You said that yesterday."
She took it before he could remind her where yesterday's tea had ended up. He stepped around a canvas and sat in the only chair she had left empty.

Beneath the invitations lay her packing list: each frame measured, each receipt numbered. She had caught an extra charge in the transport quote and made the company send a new one. Her father would have checked it the same way, one finger under each line.

Her parents ran a musical-instrument shop in New Jersey. Their last parcel had contained a box of guitar picks she had not asked for, a sweater she had left behind, and a note reminding her not to use the picks for scraping paint.
She had already used two.
"Read this once more," she said.
"I've read it."
"As if you haven't."
Mukund put down his cup. He read the date, the time, the Chicago gallery's address. Aarna watched his eyes pass over her name.
"Well?"
"Still you."
She laughed. Fourteen days. In fourteen days she would stand beside the work while strangers looked at it.
He held the invitation at arm's length. "Blue shirt?"
"You have four."
"The one you don't complain about."
"That narrows it to three."
"You wore blue the first time," she added.
Three years earlier, B(L)IND had put them at a cafe table in Chicago: a blind date with a random person. She had checked the table number twice and decided she could leave after one coffee.

His family, like hers, had come from India and settled in America. Beyond that, their answers went in different directions. Her parents were in New Jersey; she had graduated from college in New York state. He had graduated in California and moved to Chicago for work. He still said back home when he meant San Jose.
He had arrived early. She had arrived with paint on her wrist. Instead of asking what she did, he had asked what she was making.
She told him about a room whose wall changed colour after sunset. He asked what colour it became. She tried three answers. He stirred a cup that no longer needed stirring and waited for the third.
After the cups were cleared, neither reached for a coat.
They had both been in relationships before. They talked about those early on, without secrets or comparisons, and left them in the past.
"Not that blue shirt," she said now. "The other one."
He put the invitation over his face.
His phone vibrated against his leg. A hospital appointment had moved forward. He had twenty minutes less than he had thought.

Under that message was a photograph from his elder brother in San Jose: a single tomato on a kitchen scale. His brother was a software engineer and had recently become unreasonably proud of things that grew without his supervision.
Mukund sent back, "Does it come with a warranty?"

His mother, also in San Jose, had sent a voice note. She was recording a podcast later and wanted him to listen to the introduction. Most of her guests were Indian celebrities and other well-known people settled around the United States. She could spend forty minutes deciding how to introduce someone she had already spoken to for an hour.
He replied that he would listen after work, then turned the phone over.
Aarna was rubbing a fleck of paint from her thumb.

He hummed the first line of an old film song. On Sundays he listened to different recordings of it and still sang the same wrong note. Aarna's father had once offered to sell him a keyboard at cost so he could find it.
"I like this one," he said, touching the image on the invitation. Beneath it she had printed Room Enough.
"You said it looked unfinished."
"When it was unfinished."
"It hasn't changed."
He leaned closer. The pale rectangle might have been a doorway or a window. He liked the blue around it, the way it seemed to continue beyond the edge of the picture.
"Maybe I have."
She stopped picking at her thumb.
When he stood, she caught his wrist. A blue streak ran along his cuff. He looked back at the chair.
"Don't move."
"That sounds expensive."
She tried the corner of a damp cloth. He waited while she worked at the mark.
"Sorry."
"I'll tell them it's a limited edition."
At the door he took an invitation.
"You know where it is," she said.
"It's not for the address."
He put it in the inside pocket of his bag, away from the product brochures, where it would stay flat.
